content:
on November 02, 2026

LARRY WOODY
Main Street Media

A headline awhile back caught my eye: “Crossville Center of Bigfoot Universe.”

That being my hometown, I eagerly read the story. I thought that perhaps my boyhood fishing buddy Booger had been mistaken for Bigfoot.

Last time I saw Bogger he was hulking and shaggy and did a lot of growling because his dream of owning a worm ranch wasn’t working out. The worms were too hard to lasso and brand.

Or perhaps it was our old Crossville High quarterback, Hulk, who back then showed some Bigfoot characteristics, communicating by grunting and chewing with his mouth open. I still can’t understand why head cheerleader Mary Sue Wattenbarger dumped me for him.

Or perhaps the Bigfoot Universe headline was a misprint. Maybe it should have said Crossville is the center of the “Barefoot Universe.” 

A lot of us kids ran barefoot back then and still have the scars from rusty nails and broken glass to prove it.

But it’s a stretch from barefoot to Bigfoot, and the headline wasn’t a mistake. The story really was about Bigfoot. (Or Bigfeet, if there’s more than one.)

It was also tongue-in-cheek.

Every year a Bigfoot Festival is held in the Upper Cumberlands, with locals and tourists mingling for some county fair-like fun and frolic. As far as I know the guest of honor – Mr. Bigfoot — has never made an appearance.

While Crossville’s Bigfoot Festival is for amusement only, a lot of folks are convinced the big guy is out there. The national Bigfoot Research Organization data base lists 112 “confirmed” Bigfoot sightings in Tennessee in recent years.

Sightings have been reported throughout North America dating back for centuries. Indian legends and frontier folklore include accounts of a giant creature with the same modern-day descriptions.

The BRO doesn’t include sightings from witnesses who also saw Elvis eating a Whopper at Burger King or who were beamed up and probed by little green men in flying saucers.

The BRO’s sightings come from law enforcement officers, soccer moms, veteran outdoorsmen and no-nonsense ranchers and farmers. Their Bigfoot descriptions are identical, and they have no reason to fabricate and falsify.

Wildlife biologists discount the sightings. They claim they are figments of imagination or bears standing upright.

The Tennessee Wildlife Resources Agency agrees – there are no Bigfoots – but that was also its stance on cougars. For years TWRA wildlife experts adamantly insisted there were none here, but they were eventually proved wrong.

But there is empirical evidence of cougars – namely, an actual cougar – and no such evidence of a Bigfoot. No carcass or skeleton has ever been found. The only “evidence” is a few fuzzy photos and some muddy footprints that could have been made by LeBron James.

Just to be safe, the TWRA includes Bigfoot on its protected-species list. It’s illegal to harm or harass them. If one shows up at Crossville’s Bigfoot Festival, be nice to him.
